## Utah Valley University
## Evangeline M. Bollard

For my final project, I focused on breast cancer research.The average woman has a 1 in 8 chance of getting breast cancer in her lifetime. Every year, about 2 million women are diagnosed with breast cancer worldwide. Men can also get breast cancer, although these case only account for about 1% of breast cancer diagnoses in the US annually. The data set that I used for this project contains published profiling of 77 breast cancer samples generated by the Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium in partnership with the National Cancer Institute and National Institutes of Health. 

# Raw Data 
The original data set included information on each breast cancer sample taken from a patient. Other non-identifying but important attributes are also listed including: gender, diagnosis age, hormone receptor status, & tumor stage. 
    
![Figure 1. Raw data](/Users/Angie/Desktop/Data_Course_BOLLARD/Semester Project/cancer_data.png)

# Data Simplification

I simplified this data set to analyze the different stages and sub-stages of breast cancer using three therapeutic targets, Estrogen Receptors, Progesterone Receptors, and Human Epidermal growth factor receptor 2 or HER2. This approach is an effective strategy because the status of these therapeutic targets is the key factor to determine a treatment strategy for each breast cancer patient. The combination of these types creates molecular sub-types of breast cancer that each have their own best therapy treatment. 

# Cleaned Data
The resulting clean data is organized by AJCC stage (the system used to describe the extent of cancer in a patient's body) therapeutic target status, and patient count for each combination of factors.  

![Figure 2. Cleaned data](/Users/Angie/Desktop/Data_Course_BOLLARD/Semester Project/simplified_analysis_1.png)
![Figure 2. Cleaned data](/Users/Angie/Desktop/Data_Course_BOLLARD/Semester Project/simplified_analysis_2.png)

## Subtypes of Breast Cancer and Best Treatment

In Hormone Receptor positive and HER2 negative cases, hormone therapy is used because estrogen and progesterone receptors have their growth controlled by hormones. Hormone therapy can either lower estrogen or progesterone levels or by blocking the receptors entirely. 
In HER2 positive cases, the cancer cells make too much HER2 protein on their surface which allows them to grow exponentially. In these cases, the cells are treated with anti-HER2 targeted therapy that bonds to the HER2 receptors on the cancer cell surface and blocks the growth signals.
In Triple Negative Breast Cancers (ER-, PR- and HER2-), these cancer cells lack all three receptors. Because they don't have specific targets, targeted therapy doesn't work. Therefore, these cells are treated with more generalized treatments like chemotherapy or immunotherapy.

![Figure 3. Types of Breast Cancer](/Users/Angie/Desktop/Data_Course_BOLLARD/Semester Project/types_of_breast_cancer.PNG)

# Analysis
With the data in a usable format, it allows us to see the prevalence of the therapeutic sub-types at different stages of breast cancer. The most important metric for breast cancer is the presence of a therapeutic target. Some cancers do not have any of the three receptors, and therefore does not respond to hormonal or HER2 targeted therapies. These types of cancer are extremely aggressive, recur more often, and have a higher probability of mortality.

![Figure 4. Triple Negative Breast Cancer by Stage](/Users/Angie/Desktop/Data_Course_BOLLARD/Semester Project/Table of TNBC by cancer stage.png)
No conversion means there is a failure of a treatment to change the tumor's status from having unfavorable characteristics to a state where curative intervention is possible. Stage I is where there is a small, localized tumor that has not spread. Stage IIA means the cancer is advanced but has not metastasized. Stage IIB means the tumor is invasive based on size (between 2-5 cm) with a spread to 1 to 3 lymph nodes. Stage IIIA is when the cancer has spread to the lymph nodes but has not spread to distant organs. Stage IIIB means the cancer has spread into the chest wall or skin of the breast. Stage IIIC means the cancer has spread to 10 or more lymph nodes, but not distant organs. 

![Figure 5. Proportion of TNBC by Cancer Stage](/Users/Angie/Desktop/Data_Course_BOLLARD/Semester Project/Proportion of TNBC by Cancer Stage.png)



# Survivability
Another metric that was examined was the survivability of the different sub-types of breast cancer at each stage. By analyzing the data across stages and sub-stages, we can better understand how the tumor changes as the disease progresses and how that affects outcomes. The best existing model to estimate survival after treatment is called the Kaplan-Meier survival model. The KM model estimates the probability of survival over specific periods of time and is visualized with a step-wise curve. 

![Figure 6. Kaplan-Meier Survival Curves by Stage](/Users/Angie/Desktop/Data_Course_BOLLARD/Semester Project/Kaplan-Meier Survial Curves by Breast Cancer Stages.png)
This KM plot shows the overall survival probability of breast cancer patients over time based on AJCC stages. In the AJCC staging system, lower stages generally have better survival than higher stages. For example, patients that are in Stage I (yellow), Stage IIA (green) and Stage IIIB (Pink) have the highest overall survival probability. The plot mostly supports this, but there are some irregularities. The high survival rate and flat curve of Stages IIA and IIIB seems to be because of the small number of patients they represent. Stage IIB (Cyan) shows a steeper decline than the top curves, but better survival then the lowest curves. The median survival time is the point on the x-axis where the survival curve crosses 50% survival. The curves for stages I and IIA remain above this line for the entire observation period, indicating a good prognosis. The No Conversion line (red) drops below this mark at about 1500 days. Meaning a relatively short survival expectancy.
